Spirit, you name a people I have not heard—Wewush. Tell me where they lie, how many souls they hold, and how long their hunger will last, that I may weigh what we can spare.  
Our granaries hold more wheat than we shall eat this year, yet we must keep enough to see our own children through the lean months.  
If Wewush is near and their need is true, I will send a share of our xi wheat, for fairness bids us aid strangers, but I will not jeopardize the stores that keep our own hearths warm.

Spirit, you say the people of Joawethom are hungry this year. I will help them, but I must first know where they lie and how many they are, so that I can take only what we can spare without putting our own store at risk. If they are near enough for a small party to reach and return before the snows come, I will send two adults with a sack of xi wheat—enough to feed a dozen folk for a week—while we keep the rest for our own winter and planting. If the road is far or the need great, I will ask what they can give in return, be it hide, fish, or a promise of friendship, so that trade strengthens both villages. Tell me, spirit, the distance to Joawethom and the number of its hungry, and I will act accordingly.

Spirit, you speak of neighbours at Joawethom who are hungry. I have never heard of that place, and we have not yet met any other village. If they truly need grain, we have plenty stored—more than enough to feed our own people through the lean months. But before we send any of our stores, I would know how far Joawethom lies, how many weeks of hunger they face, and what they might give in return. Without that information I cannot risk sending away food that may be needed here when winter comes. Tell me more, spirit, and I will decide.
